input: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, and the results that were obtained are presented in this passage. At a temperature of 300 K, the value of $k$ was 0.015 s-1, whereas at a temperature of 340 K the value of $k$ was 1.325 s-1, although it should be noted that this second value was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 95 kJ mol-1 and therefore represents a derived value rather than a directly measured one. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%, which provides an indication of the reproducibility of the measurements that were carried out. It is also important to note that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, and the reason for this is that above 340 K the solvent was observed to evaporate during the sampling process, which meant that reliable measurements could no longer be obtained in that region. The relative standard deviation of 4% was established from the triplicate measurements carried out at 300 K and at 340 K, and it applies to the measurements at both of the temperatures that were studied in the course of this work. Taken together, the results show a very substantial increase in the rate constant between 300 K and 340 K, spanning the interval over which measurements could be made, although the upper end of that interval is represented by a value that was obtained by calculation rather than by direct measurement.
target: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.015 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 1.325 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 95 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. No rate constant is reported above 340 K: above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, so samples taken at higher temperatures did not hold the composition the measurement requires, and no value from them is quoted. The increase between the two temperatures is large, and its upper end is a derived end. The value at 340 K rests on the Arrhenius relation and the stated activation energy, not on a measurement of the same standing as the value at 300 K, and the pair of values should be read with that difference in standing kept in view. The triplicate measurements fix the scatter of $k$ at each temperature at the stated 4%, and that scatter bounds the precision with which either value can be quoted. A derived value is not a weaker value for being derived, but it is a different kind of value: it inherits the uncertainty of the activation energy and of the relation itself, on top of the scatter the triplicate measurements record, and it cannot be checked against a sample in the way the measured value can. That difference in kind is stated wherever the pair is used. The reported pair therefore covers the interval from 300 K to 340 K and no more. The limit at the top of the interval is set by the sampling failure, not by the reaction: the reaction continues above 340 K, but the method used here returns no rate constant there.
